title: Inquest set into Watson Lake man's death
article: The Yukon's chief coroner has scheduled an inquest into the death of a Watson Lake man who stopped breathing in an RCMP cell over a year ago.
Sharon Hanley announced the inquest this morning. It's scheduled for two or three days in Watson Lake beginning May 23.
Freddie Stewart, 36, died in the Watson Lake detachment cell after having been arrested for public intoxication in March 2000.

Hanley was just made the chief coroner last month after having served as the acting chief coroner through two years and four inquests. She said this afternoon that the inquest is being held as soon as possible.
"It's tough sometimes, and I would like to get them done sooner, but there are so many things that go into an inquest."
She cited witness availability as a big part of the delay in scheduling inquests.
Still, within about a year, while hard on the family, is a reasonable time frame, she said.
Holding an inquest is required whenever a prisoner dies in cells.
"We always try to hold (the inquest) in the community where it happened, because those are the people who are affected the most."
While inquests are not fault-finding or criminal proceedings, Hanley said they can be useful in preventing future deaths and in providing the public with accurate information surrounding the death.
Another inquest, into the death of Madeleine Henry, has yet to be scheduled.
Henry, 41, fell unconscious in Whitehorse RCMP cells last May and never regained consciousness, dying two weeks later.
Stewart was arrested outside Tags Food and Gas, brought to the Watson Lake RCMP detachment and put in a cell at just past midnight on March 18, 2000.

Officers found Stewart in his cell 2 1/2 hours later, apparently not breathing. CPR was commenced immediately in an attempt to resuscitate Stewart. However, all efforts to revive the prisoner were unsuccessful, a police statement said at the time.
An ambulance was dispatched and Stewart was brought to the Watson Lake Hospital where, at 4:12 a.m., he was pronounced dead by the attending doctor.
Stewart's death was the second in RCMP cells in three months.
The previous Dec. 25, another Watson Lake man, John Tibbett Jr., 38, was found dead in his Whitehorse RCMP cell, having hung himself.
In March 1995, 40-year-old Robert Keddie died while in custody in Whitehorse of a drug overdose complicated by alcohol.
Like Tibbett and Stewart, Keddie was originally arrested on an alcohol-related charge.
Stewart's cell did have a camera and a guard was on duty.
Both the coroner and the RCMP will be holding separate investigations into the incident, though foul play is not suspected.
Stewart, who would have celebrated his 37th birthday the day after he died, was known to police and had a long history of minor, non-violent offences.
Pat Irvin, owner of Watson Lake's Belvedere Hotel, also knew Stewart.
"He was not allowed to drink in any of our bars," he said at the time. "He might come in to socialize, but as soon as he becomes a nuisance, he's out. We don't serve him."
